# Submitting a Session

If you presented a session, or are about to, your material can go on this site as a chapter with your name on it.

**You do not need a GitHub account, Git, or any software installed.** Send the files to an editor and they will do the rest. That is the whole process — the rest of this page is detail.

---

## What to send

Whatever you already have. There is no required format, and you do not need to convert anything before sending.

- **Slides** — PowerPoint, Keynote, PDF, Google Slides
- **Notebooks** — Jupyter or Colab `.ipynb`
- **Code** — R or Python scripts, in whatever state they ran in
- **Data** — the files your examples use, if they can be shared
- **Notes** — an outline, a draft, or a handout

Send the originals rather than exports where you have a choice; an editor can extract images from a `.pptx` but cannot get them back out of a flattened PDF at usable quality.

If you happen to write in Quarto or R Markdown already, send the `.qmd` or `.Rmd` and it will need almost no conversion. Nobody expects this.^[`.qmd` is "Quarto Markdown" — plain text with light formatting marks, where `**bold**` becomes **bold** and `# Heading` becomes a heading. It is what the chapters on this site are written in.]

## What we need from you

Three things, in the email:

1. **Your name as you want it published.** This appears under the chapter title, in the sidebar, and in the PDF. Spelling and form are yours to choose.
2. **The session date.** Chapters are ordered by when the session happened, not when the material arrives.
3. **An email address for the credit trail** — the one you want attached to the published record.

If your session used data that cannot be shared, say so, and the chapter will use a synthetic or public substitute instead.

## What happens next

1. An editor converts the material into a chapter — slides become prose with the figures kept, notebook cells become readable code blocks.
2. It goes on the site under your name, with the session date, in both the web version and the PDF.
3. You get a link, and you check it. **This step matters** — you are the only person who can confirm the author line, the date, and that nothing was mangled in conversion. Say so and it gets fixed.

Editing is for format, not content. If something needs cutting or rewriting, an editor will ask you first.

Turnaround is usually a week or two, faster outside the end of a semester.

## Questions people ask

**Does my material have to be polished?** No. Rough notes and working code are normal — most chapters started that way.

**Can I update it later?** Yes. Send the changes to an editor whenever.

**Can I take it down?** Yes, no explanation needed.

**Who owns it?** You wrote it and you are credited as the author. The site's licensing terms are still being settled — if that matters to you, say so and it will be part of the conversation.

**Can I write the chapter myself?** If you would rather do the whole thing — write it in Quarto and publish it directly — that means joining as an editor: repository access, and an afternoon of setup. Say so and we will walk you through it. Most presenters would rather not, which is exactly why the send-us-the-files route exists.

- **Sara Mohammadi** — content review, editorial standards
